What we mean by “The Talk”

The one about how you want to die. Yes, it's the scary one — which is exactly why we'd rather have it early, gently, and with a few laughs.

Walking on eggshells? Let's crack yolks. Life's a big joke.

Most of us walk into dying — our own, or someone we love's — unprepared. Not because we don't care. Because nobody ever showed us how.

How could you've known what you've never been shown?

So we keep it polite. We talk about the weather. We say “you look great.” The person in the bed says “I'm fine” and “I don't want to be a burden.” The family says “we're staying strong for them.” Everyone protects everyone's feelings, and nobody wants to go first. The real stuff gets saved for later — but we only know it was the last time once it's already passed.

Life gives grief. We give Grace.

We're not saying stop fighting. We're talking about a different kind of fight — the fight to be heard, to have “The Talk,” and to make sure every hard conversation starts soft, not harsh.

Now, here is the purpose of this circus

Consider this your permission slip: you don't have to be fearless — just a little brave, a little early. Somebody has to go first. May it be you.

That's why we started Golden Soul Circus:

to celebrate patients' rights, lighten the caregiver's load, and rehearse “The Talk” with you — calmly, kindly, with room to laugh — before “later” becomes an emergency room.

A circus with a purpose.

Founded by Nashville hospice nurses Brad & Cass Burns.

Golden Soul Circus was founded by hospice nurses who've sat with hundreds of deaths — the beautiful ones and the devastating ones. A decade in Med-Surg, ICU, float pool, and covid units taught what none of those units had time for: that the dying, and everyone who loves them, deserve to rehearse the goodbye, not just survive it.

Palliative PAL

Home Caregiver Training

For family caregivers, friends, volunteers and doulas. No medical background needed.

Join the list

Real hospice skills, taught online by two hospice nurses, at your own pace. Seven short modules, about 6½ hours in all, and every lesson is under 10 minutes, so you can learn a few minutes at a time.

  • Welcome to the Big Top — how it works, and building your “Know Your Team” page.
  • Empowered Essentials — moving, bathing and feeding your person safely, with dignity.
  • Mindful Medicine — keeping a medicine list, the three questions to ask, and what to watch for.
  • Vital Signs and Vibes — pulse, breathing and home devices, plus reading the person behind the numbers.
  • Sacred Space and Heavenly Hygiene — clean, dry, re-apply, and a room that feels like theirs.
  • Soul Care as Self-Care — spotting burnout and refilling your own well.
  • Walking Each Other Home — a full day of care, start to finish.

Every module ends with practice on your own “Doris” (a pillow works) and a short, untimed Flower Check. Each one earns a petal; six petals complete your flower and unlock your Palliative PAL Certificate of Completion. You also finish with your own Care Binder and a full set of pocket cards.

Sliding-scale pricing, with free seats for family caregivers in need.

A guided hour for families to share what usually goes unsaid. Led by hospice nurses. No pressure to speak.

1. Toast — Everyone shares one thing they love about the person. Kind words, out loud, while they can hear them.

2. Roast — A gentle, honest nudge. What do the people who love you most wish you'd do?

3. Prost — The last word. What would you say if you knew it was your last chance?

Bring a photo of the old version of you that you're ready to lay to rest. We'll give it a proper send-off.

Give your people this hour.

See the full show

Reiki energy healing mixed with subtle circus-style pomp and circumstance facilitated by sacred and silly psychopomps, a nuanced healing ceremony for any home.

What is Reiki?

Reiki (say it RAY-kee) is a gentle practice from Japan. We rest our hands lightly on you, or just above you, while you relax. Many people tell us it helps them slow down, breathe easier and sleep better. After a loss, that kind of rest can be hard to find.

What is a psychopomp?

A psychopomp (say it SY-ko-pomp) is a guide who helps someone through the passage of death. Cultures all over the world tell stories about them. As hospice nurses, we do this work at the bedside, and we bring the same care to the families who are still here.

What happens during the visit

  1. We sit down together and talk about what feels heavy.
  2. We move through your home, room by room, with Reiki and sound bowls.
  3. We close with a small ceremony to let go of what is ready to leave: grief, old habits or a hard season.

Who comes to your home

We hold Reiki Level 4 mastery. As bedside nurses, we are trained to notice how a room feels and to help it settle.

Reiki is complementary care. It does not replace medical treatment.

Ready to clear the air at home?

“The Talk” is the conversation about what someone wants near the end of life: comfort, care, who makes decisions, and what matters most.

Most of us were raised to keep the peace. So we say “I'm fine,” don't want to be a burden, and save the hard stuff for later. Later keeps getting shorter.

Doctors often won't bring it up first. That leaves it to you, and it's easier with someone in the room who's done this hundreds of times.

We call the “keep-everyone-happy” habit the “People-Pleasedome.” You're welcome to leave anytime.

You don't have to start it alone.

ABOUT US

A circus with a purpose.

Founded by Nashville hospice nurses Brad & Cass Burns.

Who we are

We're all nurses — just some of us are registered.

Brad

Brad calls himself a golden soul retriever: raised by singing telegrams, trained on the stage, and carried from acting into nursing. He grew up afraid of hospitals — big buildings that left him feeling small — and spent years inside them anyway, in Med-Surg, ICU, float pool, covid, and wound care. In hospice he found the job where he gets to tell the truth every day, and he brings the stagecraft with him: improv, music, dance, juggling, and a sacred-and-silly way of meeting people wherever the ground is shifting under them. Licensed in 2016, he is in his 10th year as a nurse.

Cass

Cass has most recently served patients of earth in end-of-life (EOL) care. After a journey through all categories of ICU nursing, including burn, trauma, covid, and a range of medical and surgical units, Cass left the critical care setting for more holistic and intimate care in integrative wellness and home hospice nursing. Over 10+ years of patient and community care, Cass has witnessed the full spectrum of quality lives and deaths. She is honored to share those findings in a welcoming and joyful manner to open minds and hearts around health and wellness, life and death.

It’s all sacred, it’s all silly, it’s all safe.

One of her patients, silent for days, once looked up as she reached his bedside and asked, “Are you free?” She answered: “Yes, I am, brother — and so are you.”
